chapter_theme: Ainkurunuru 31 to 40, the marutham decade spoken to the friend: by our reading the other woman's voice throughout, holding the lord to an oath sworn at the bathing ford, mocking his wives who weep a week for one day's absence, watching her own eyes and skin turn the colour of the water lily as he forgets her, and hearing at last that he has settled back in his wives' town, where the leaping fish opens the closed lily.

31.reading: The other woman asks her friend whether the lord will now say he owes nothing on the oath he swore at the great ford of their town, by the old bent marutham tree, in front of the band of women bathing together.
31.nuance: The oath's only witnesses are the bathing companions (உடனாடு ஆயம்), not a god; her fear is not that he will break it but that he will call it no debt at all (கடனன்று), which a human witness cannot prevent.

32.reading: The other woman tells her friend that, they say, for the one day the lord came to her house his women weep for seven, melting quickly like wax held to fire.
32.nuance: The arithmetic (ஒருநாள் ... எழுநாள்) is the mockery: one visit costs the wives a week of tears, and the wax simile makes their grief look soft and helpless rather than wronged.

33.reading: The other woman tells her friend that, they say, the lord bathes with women at the great ford where the marutham trees stand tall among spread flowers, so that his cool-garlanded chest is taken by one after another.
33.nuance: தலைத்தலைக் கொள: his chest passes from hand to hand like a shared float; she reports it as hearsay (என்ப), so the jealousy is hers but the evidence is the town's.

34.reading: The other woman tells her friend that her eyes, grown pale for a man who is a stranger to her, have taken the colour of the pollen of the hollow-stalked water lily in their town's pond.
34.nuance: ஏதிலாளர் (a stranger, one with no tie) is bitter: the man she pales for has no bond to her that anyone would recognise, so even her pallor has no rightful claim.

comparisons.tenor: the yellow pallor of her eyes

35.reading: The other woman tells her friend that her dark beauty once glowed even beyond the colour of the soft, fibre-peeled stalk of the water lily in their town's pond, and now it has turned pale.
35.nuance: மன்னே marks a state that is over: the comparison is of what she was, and the last line, which recurs in Ainkurunuru 144, closes it with the present pallor.

36.reading: The other woman tells her friend that if the man of the town can forget them and be content, they too could forget him and be content, if only her kohl-lined eyes, once taken for carp, did not give way to pallor.
36.nuance: The will to forget is claimed in full (அமைகுவம்) and then taken back by the body: the condition she cannot meet is her own eyes, so the pride of the first lines is undone by the last.

37.reading: The other woman tells her friend that the lord, who makes the kohl-lined eyes of those who loved him pale and brim with tears, is skilled, truly skilled, at lying, and never shows the oath he swore to be true.
37.nuance: வல்லன் வல்லன் is ironic praise: his one proven skill is deceit, and the paling, streaming eyes of those who trusted him are the evidence against his oath.

38.reading: The other woman tells her friend that the lord never cares for those who understood and trusted his word, for he left her weeping, she whose body outshines cool young leaves and whose forearm wears a bright bangle.
38.nuance: Line 4's half-line (ஒள்தொடி முன்கை யாம் அழப் பிரிந்து) recurs in 40, where it leads to where he went; here it leads only to the charge that he forgets those who believed him.

39.reading: The other woman tells her friend that the man of the town, who once embraced her so close that her warm breasts pressed against him, has left so that her bamboo-smooth jewelled shoulders grow slack, though once he was a man who would never leave.
39.nuance: The last line can be read two ways: 'though he has left, he was once one who never left' (மன்னே of a past state), or 'though he has left, he does not leave (my heart)'; the first is taken here.

40.reading: The other woman tells her friend that, they say, the lord of the land where the leaping kendai fish opens the water lily that the bees had waited on has left her weeping and settled in the town of his wives.
40.nuance: The closing epithet answers the news: as the fish's leap opens the closed lily, his coming home opens his wives, the same wives who in 32 melted for a week over one day's absence.

links.note: Both end on the same words, உற்ற சூளே, an oath sworn at the broad ford of 'our town'; in Kuruntokai 53 the friend says it was sworn holding the girl's forearm with the hill goddesses as witness and now afflicts them, in Ainkurunuru 31 the other woman says it was sworn before the bathing companions and asks whether he will call it no debt.
links.teaches: The witness decides what a broken ford-oath costs: sworn before goddesses it turns into a danger that falls on the women, sworn before human bathers it shrinks to a debt the man can simply disown, so the courtesan's oath is the weaker for lacking a god.

links.note: In Ainkurunuru 31 the other woman holds the lord to an oath he swore her at the bathing ford; in Akananuru 166 the same kind of lord swears to his wife by the god of Velur that he never bathed with the other woman, and the courtesan asks who then held the float with her yesterday.
links.teaches: Held together, the two show the marutham lord's oaths cancelling each other: the bathing he swore by to the courtesan is the bathing he forswears to his wife, so one of the two oaths must be false and each woman is left holding an oath the other's makes worthless.

links.note: Both put the courtesan's report of the wives in the same formula: அழுப என்ப அவன் பெண்டிர் (they say his women weep) in Ainkurunuru 32, கழறுப என்ப அவன் பெண்டிர் (they say his women rail) in Akananuru 76.
links.teaches: The one formula frames the wives two ways, as melting in tears like wax or as clamouring like a bard's drum, and the courtesan's answer scales with it, from a mocking count of days in the short poem to an open vow to hold him by force in the long one.

links.note: Ainkurunuru 36 says that if he forgets them, they too could forget and be content, were it not that her eyes go pale; Kural 1207 has the woman say she does not know forgetting, and even remembering burns.
links.teaches: The Sangam speaker claims forgetting is in her power and lays the failure on her paling eyes, while the Kural woman denies she can forget at all, so the older poem places love's hold in the body against the will and the couplet moves it into the mind itself.

links.note: Ainkurunuru 37 has நயந்தோர் உண்கண் பசந்துபனி மல்க, the eyes of those who loved him pale and brimming; Kural 1232 has நயந்தவர் ... பசந்து பனிவாரும் கண், pale eyes streaming that seem to tell of the beloved's unkindness.
links.teaches: Valluvar keeps the Ainkurunuru's very words for the pale, wet eyes but changes their office: in the Sangam poem they are evidence the wronged woman cites against his lying oath, in the couplet they become speakers that publish his unkindness to others, so the image moves from accusation to involuntary gossip.

source_issues: The colophon of every poem in this decade gives thinai only, no thurai; the speaker (the other woman) is inferred from 32 and 40 and recorded in thurai_akam with a note.
38 line 4 reads ஒள்தோடி where the same half-line in 40 line 2 reads ஒள்தொடி; தோடி is likely a misprint for தொடி (bangle).
38 line 3 writes வெளவும் with the two-part vowel sign (ெ + ள) rather than ௌ; it is the verb வௌவும்.
37 line 4 divides the words as சூள்வாய்த் தல்லே, for சூள் வாய்த்தல்லே.
33 line 3 என்பதன் is likely என்ப + தன் written together.
